prompt: Why do most full-range loudspeakers use two or more drivers with a crossover?

options.text: Because a driver large enough for bass beams and breaks up at high frequencies, and a small tweeter can't handle bass excursion
options.explanation: Correct. Splitting the band lets each driver work where it performs well.

options.text: To make the speaker look more expensive
options.explanation: There are real acoustic reasons: no single driver covers the whole band well.

options.text: Because amplifiers can only drive one frequency at a time
options.explanation: Amplifiers handle the whole audio band at once.
Impedance isn't the reason; the crossover is about frequency ranges.

workedExample:
A big cone moves enough air for bass, but it starts to **beam** (focus its sound into a narrowing forward beam) once the wavelength gets close to the cone size. A rough guide to where that starts:

```formula
f_beam ≈ c / (2πa)
f_beam ≈ (343 m/s) / (2π × 0.065 m)
f_beam ≈ 840 Hz
where
f_beam: the frequency above which the cone starts to beam, in hertz (Hz)
c: the speed of sound in air, about 343 metres per second (m/s) at 20 °C
π: pi, about 3.14159
a: the cone's effective radius (half its diameter), in metres (m); here 0.065 m for a 13 cm cone
≈: approximately equal to
m: metres
s: seconds
Hz: hertz, cycles per second
In words: bigger cones beam at lower frequencies; a 13 cm woofer already narrows its dispersion above about 840 Hz, and it breaks up higher still.
```

A small dome tweeter disperses treble widely but can't make the large excursion bass needs. A crossover routes lows to the woofer and highs to the tweeter, so each driver works where it performs well.

prompt: What asymptotic stopband slope does a conventional fourth-order Butterworth or Linkwitz–Riley low-pass filter have?
workedExample:
Each order (pole) of a conventional filter adds 6 dB/octave of asymptotic slope:

```formula
slope = 6n dB/octave
slope = 4 × 6 dB/octave
slope = 24 dB/octave
where
slope: how fast the output falls far into the stopband, in decibels per octave
n: the filter order, here 4
dB: decibel, a logarithmic measure of level ratio; −6 dB is about half the voltage
octave: a doubling of frequency
In words: a fourth-order filter falls four times as steeply as a first-order one: 24 dB for each doubling of frequency.
```

The 6 dB comes from a first-order filter halving its voltage each octave far from the corner (the same slope is often quoted as 20 dB per decade, a tenfold frequency change). So 1st order is 6, 2nd is 12, 3rd is 18 and 4th is 24 dB/octave.

prompt: What's the main difference between a passive and an active crossover?

options.text: Passive crossovers need mains power; active ones don't
options.explanation: It's the reverse: passive networks need no power; active ones contain powered electronics.

options.text: Active crossovers only work with subwoofers
options.explanation: Active crossovers are used for every band, from studio monitor loudspeakers to PA systems.

options.text: There's no difference in where they sit in the chain
options.explanation: Where they sit is the defining difference.

options.text: Passive crossovers sit after one power amp at speaker level; active crossovers filter at line level before a separate amp for each driver

workedExample:
```
passive: amp -> LC network -> drivers
active:  filters -> amp per driver
```

Active and DSP crossovers aren't affected by driver impedance and can add delay, EQ and limiting per driver.
